aiAgentFacts.fact: In a random sample of 22,333 UK dogs under primary veterinary care in 2016, the one-year period prevalence of a recorded periodontal disease diagnosis was 12.52% (95% CI 12.09–12.97).

Primary-care practices, where diagnosis rests largely on visual assessment of conscious dogs, report average prevalences of 9.3-18.2%, while detailed examinations of anaesthetised dogs report 44-100% — a large detection gap.

Eighteen breeds showed increased odds of periodontal disease versus crossbred dogs; the highest were Toy Poodle (OR 3.97), King Charles Spaniel (2.63), Greyhound (2.58) and Cavalier King Charles Spaniel (2.39).
Increasing adult bodyweight was associated with progressively decreasing odds of periodontal disease — smaller dogs carry higher risk, contrary to common owner assumption.
Brachycephalic breeds had 1.25 times the odds (95% CI 1.11-1.42) and spaniel types 1.63 times the odds (95% CI 1.42-1.87) of periodontal disease compared with their reference groups.
The 12.52% figure counts diagnoses recorded in clinical notes, not disease present in mouths; undiagnosed disease is by construction absent from it.
No owner-observable sign was evaluated as a screening test in this study; halitosis and similar signs have no established sensitivity or specificity here.
Neither study evaluated any prevention strategy — brushing, diet, chews and professional cleaning frequency were not tested as interventions.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by these papers. The breed and bodyweight findings do support proactively raising dental assessment for small-breed, spaniel-type, brachycephalic and older dogs rather than waiting for an owner complaint.
redFlags: Not addressed — neither study identifies red-flag findings or urgency thresholds.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the cohort study measures recorded periodontal disease diagnoses and does not evaluate other causes of oral signs.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The detection-gap comparison implies that conscious visual assessment substantially under-detects relative to detailed examination under anaesthesia; the review reports both figures but neither paper issues a screening protocol.

limitations: The primary outcome is a recorded diagnosis, not disease presence — the study measures what primary care detects, and undiagnosed disease is invisible to it by construction
Breed and size odds may partly reflect differential examination rates rather than true incidence; a record-based design cannot separate detection intensity from occurrence
The 44-100% anaesthetised-examination range is drawn from studies with differing populations, grading systems and eras — appropriate as order-of-magnitude context, not as a precise figure
No prevention or treatment intervention was evaluated by either paper
Severity distribution is not reported at the level used here, so 'diagnosed' spans everything from mild gingivitis to advanced periodontitis
